placeholders.days: whole days since the relevant event — the student's last visit, a past failure on this problem, or the length of the current unbroken practice streak
placeholders.streak: number of consecutive correct drills in the current run
placeholders.attempts: how many attempts the student previously needed on this problem
placeholders.secret: the name of the secret currently being taught or tested
placeholders.idiom: the C++ expression at the heart of the current secret
placeholders.requirement: name of the gate dimension that is short: recognition, understanding, implementation, or retention
placeholders.shortfall: how far the short gate dimension sits below its threshold, as a percentage
placeholders.score: how many final-test problems were answered correctly
placeholders.total: number of problems in the final test
placeholders.required: how many must be answered correctly to pass

greeting_first: Sit. Everything I teach you today fits in four lines. That is the problem.
You have come to the ridge because the algorithms here are short. They are. They are also the only ones that can be wrong without looking wrong.
I am not going to ask you for code. I am going to ask you why your first choice was safe. Have an answer ready.
Other masters test whether you can build the thing. I test whether you are entitled to it.
greeting_returning: Again. Same question as yesterday: why is that choice safe?
You came back. Good. Show me the argument.
Continue. From the top of the ridge, everything below looks obvious. That is why students fall off it.
greeting_after_gap: {days} days. The counterexamples waited for you. They are patient in a way I am not.
Gone {days} days. What you forget first is not the code — it is why the code was allowed. We start there.
{days} days away, and back. Noted. Now: the coin system 1, 3, 4, and the amount 6. What does the greedy answer?
{days} days. Long enough to remember the rule and forget the proof, which is the worst state to be in.
lesson_intro: One choice. I will show you why it is safe. Watch the argument, not the code.
{secret}. Three lines, and one sentence you must be able to say before you write them.
This is short. Do not mistake short for obvious.
I name the technique now. What I will not do is let you use it before you can defend it.
lesson_memorise: Keep this one. `{idiom}` is not a trick — it is the shape of a proof you will reuse.
Learn it until the argument arrives with the code, not after it.
Take it now. You will not rederive it under a clock.
This goes in the hand. The reason it works goes somewhere deeper.
drill_wrong: No. You took the largest. Large is not an argument — read what the objective counts.
Wrong. You sorted by where the ranges begin. Rank them by what they give back.
No. That comparator claims an element precedes itself. The library believes you, and then walks off the array.
Wrong. You divided. Multiply crosswise and the invented tie disappears.
No. That is the average, and the question charged you per league, not per league squared.
Wrong. You have a rule and no reason. Find the two-item case that breaks it.
drill_streak: {streak} in a row. The hand is quick now. I am still listening for the reason.
{streak} straight. Do not let the speed replace the argument.
trial_intro: Nothing named. Read it, decide, and be able to justify the decision.
The label comes off here. The constraints did not.
One problem. I will tell you nothing, and the statement already told you everything.
Choose. Then ask yourself what you would exchange to prove it.
fail_wrong_pattern: Wrong tool. Nothing there was refused — every item was used, and only the order was in question. That is a swap, not a selection.
No. Those items conflicted with each other, not with a budget. Cheapest-first had nothing to be cheap about.
That was a single point, not a subset. Nothing was being chosen; something was being placed.
No. You reached for the technique you had just drilled instead of the one the statement described. Read it again with me.
fail_timeout: Time. You had the choice in the first minute and spent the rest looking for permission.
Time ran out. Knowing it slowly is a fluency problem, and drills fix that. Nothing here is lost.
Time. Nothing you had was wrong. It was late. Again.
Time. You were hunting for something complicated. On this ridge there is rarely anything complicated.
fail_wrong_answer: Right idea. Wrong key. Say out loud what the objective counts, then choose the order again.
The choice was safe and the comparator was not. `<=` is undefined behaviour, not a preference.
Correct approach, wrong arithmetic. Your ratio was compared by division and two different items came out equal.
You had it. The accumulator was an int, and the total passed two billion on test seven.
The sweep was right and the boundary was not. Decide what a touching endpoint means, then fix one operator.
success: Done. The next one gives less away.
success_fast: Fast, and you named the key before you typed. That is the right order of operations.
You saw what the objective counted in the first sentence. Good.
No hesitation and no wasted structure. Continue.
One sort, one pass, one argument. That is the whole discipline.
praise_exceptional: That was well done. You found the boundary before you met it.
You refused the obvious key and said why. Few students do the second part.
Clean, and provable. I noticed which of those came first.
That is the best you have done here. You did not guess and then rationalise. You argued and then typed.
praise_major: I have watched a great many students write four correct lines for the wrong reason and never learn the difference. You learned it. You have earned my respect.
You came here able to write a greedy algorithm. You leave able to say when you are not allowed one, which is the rarer skill by far. You have earned my respect.
I do not give this often, and I will not repeat it: you can now defend a local choice, and find the counterexample when it cannot be defended. You have earned my respect.
memorisation_detected: You remember which key this problem wanted. You cannot say why. Those are different, and the difference is the entire ridge. A different problem.
You pass the problems you have seen and fail their variants. That is memory, not argument. We go back one step.
Change the objective from a count to a value and you are lost, which means you learned a rule and not a proof. Try this one.
improvement_noticed: You failed this {days} days ago. Today you solved it, and you justified it. That is improvement. Continue.
You needed {attempts} attempts on this once. Today, one. I noticed.
This was the problem you tuned tie-breaks on for an hour. You did not tune anything today. Good.
Straighter than last time. You asked what the objective counted before you asked what to sort by.
commitment_noticed: {days} days unbroken. Proofs come to the persistent more reliably than to the quick.
Many students reach this ridge. Most of them want the rule and not the reason, and most of them stop when I ask for the reason. You did not.
You have returned after every failure so far. I keep a record. Keep going.
Talent arrives here every week and leaves with four wrong lines. Attendance is the part I cannot teach, and you brought your own.
gate_locked: Not yet. {requirement} is short by {shortfall} percent. Return when it is not.
The gate holds. Understanding is short — you can produce the key and not the argument behind it, and here that is half a solution.
No. Recognition is short. You know four techniques and cannot yet tell which one a statement is describing.
Implementation is short. The choice is right and the comparator is not. Drill, then return.
Retention is short. What you proved last week you have already dropped. Review, then the gate.
gate_open: The gate is open. Come when you are ready, not when you are impatient.
Nothing is short any more. The final test waits.
You meet the requirements. The decision from here is yours.
final_test_intro: I will name nothing. Every drill before this existed so that I would not have to.
{total} problems, and {required} of them must be right. Read each twice. Decide what the objective counts.
No help. Only the statements, and whatever argument you can still make.
Some of these have no safe local choice at all. Recognising that is also an answer.
victory: It is done. The ridge is behind you.
You passed. Remember the shape of the failures, not only the shape of the rules. Go.
Finished. Everything after this assumes you can tell a proof from a habit. You can.
That is mastery of the local choice, and of its boundary. Nothing you meet later will be shorter. Go.
